chunks.text: Queen sago is a palm-like cycad — not a true palm, but a gymnosperm related to conifers — found in the wild only in southern India, across Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, with Sri Lanka also sometimes listed as part of its native range (it is that island's only native gymnosperm). For a long time the name was applied loosely to similar-looking cycads across Southeast Asia and the Pacific, but those plants have since been reclassified: Indonesian and New Guinean populations are now called Cycas rumphii, and Philippine plants are their own species, so the name 'Cycas circinalis' in older gardening literature should be read with caution. It is widely grown in warm climates such as Hawaii as a landscaping and interior plant and for its cut feathery foliage. Its seeds are a cautionary tale in processing: they are described as poisonous in the raw state, and while repeated soaking is said to leach out the toxin enough for the flour to be used in traditional porridge or flatbread, the water from even the first soak is reportedly potent enough to kill birds and livestock that drink it, so this is not a safe food-preparation shortcut to attempt casually. Cycad toxins of this general type have also been investigated for a possible link to a neurodegenerative illness historically reported on Guam, although the cycad involved there has since been identified as a distinct species, Cycas micronesica, so the connection to queen sago itself is unconfirmed. The IUCN currently lists Cycas circinalis as Endangered.

chunks.source: LLIFLE Encyclopedia of Palms and Cycads — Cycas circinalis
chunks.text: This horticultural encyclopedia gives the morphological detail that general sources lack. The trunk is thick and unbranched, reaching about 7 metres, wrapped in corky bark whose grooves — scars from long-fallen leaf bases — are sometimes used by growers as a natural mount for epiphytic orchids. The crown carries a rosette of feathery leaves up to 2.7 metres long, each bearing roughly 54 to 110 narrow leaflets; new growth emerges with a waxy blue-grey bloom and a dense coat of fine hairs that wears off as the leaf matures. Like all cycads it is dioecious, meaning individual plants are strictly male or female: male cones are large, cylindrical structures up to nearly half a metre long, while female plants bear no true cone at all but instead cluster their ovules on loosely arranged, leaf-like megasporophylls, each capable of carrying up to fourteen seeds. The ovules themselves can reach roughly 6 centimetres, unusually large for a seed plant. Natural populations are confined to seasonally dry forests and rocky outcrops in southern India, habitat that the entry estimates has been more than halved by clearing for agriculture and settlement, with the decline expected to continue. Beyond its role as a florist's foliage and landscape specimen, the entry notes that mature plants are sometimes felled specifically to extract the starchy pith from the trunk, a destructive harvesting practice it flags as one of the species' main ongoing threats in the wild.
